To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) immigration is associated with lower local unemployment rates; 2) this is partly explained by the fact that immigration is associated with higher local labour force participation rates; and 3) the effects are not very strong and not statistically significant when we control for other factors that influence local labour markets.
the crowding out effects of immigration in the UK are small, but significant.
immigration has a negative impact on local employment and wages, but that the effects of immigration are not significantly stronger in areas that have a higher concentration of immigrants.

the impact of immigration on the labour markets of the United Kingdom.

the impact of immigrants on the UK labour market and, more generally, the effects of immigration on the UK economy.

the crowding out effects are small but not negligible, and that they are not likely to be offset by the positive impact of immigration on the economy as a whole, at least not in the short to medium term.
the effects of immigration on the local labour markets in the UK, in terms of the effects on wages and unemployment, are not strong.

immigration is not a major factor in driving internal migration in the UK, and the net effect on unemployment, wages, and the fiscal balance of regions is likely to be positive.
immigrants do not have a large effect on the labour market in their host regions, although the effects are negative.

the UK labour market is quite mobile.
